newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: TENNIS-WOODIES CLINCH TIE FOR AUSTRALIA OVER FRANCE.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-WOODIES CLINCH TIE FOR AUSTRALIA OVER FRANCE.

text.p: Australians Todd Woodbridge and Mark Woodforde, the world's leading tennis duo, on Saturday ended France's brief reign as Davis Cup champions by winning the decisive doubles match in their World Group first round tie.
Woodbridge and Woodforde, winners of 42 career titles together, defeated the French pair of Guy Forget and Guillaume Raoux 7-6 (8-6) 6-4 6-3, to hand Australia an unbeatable 3-0 lead in the tie.
The win by the Australian pair, known as "the Woodies", ended France's reign as champions after they had fought back to beat Sweden 3-2 in a dramatic final in Malmo nine weeks ago.
This time the combination of sweltering heat on a White City grass court and determined opponents proved too much for the Frenchmen.
"Last year we won after a wonderful ride and a beautiful mystery. Now, this is reality," France captain Yannick Noah later told reporters.
"If you win one year and then don't make it to the finals the next year, it is because you lost to a better team."
The doubles match started as a tense affair, with Forget and Raoux battling to stave off defeat for France after losses in the opening two singles matches on Friday.
However, the Australians gradually began to pull ahead after winning a close first set tie-breaker.

The experience of the Australian pair, the reigning Wimbledon, U.S., Australian and Olympic doubles champions, proved insurmountable for the Frenchmen, whose service games began to deteriorate as the match wore on.
Raoux cracked first when he lost a point on his serve in the first set tie-breaker, with Forget then dropping his serve in the first game of the second set.
"Once we got ahead, it was just put the foot on the pedal and put them away," Woodbridge later told reporters.
Forget agreed, describing the first set as crucial.
"Overall they were more consistent than we were and they deserved to win," he said.
Australia's win came after the 26-time winner was relegated to the event's regional competition two years ago.

Their victory in the tie was set on Friday, when Patrick Rafter fought back after losing the first two sets to beat French number one Cedric Pioline. Woodforde then downed Arnaud Boetsch in straight sets.
"If you look at it and see 3-0 you could say it was easy, but that first match was the key," Noah said.
Australia will play their second round tie in the 16-team competition in Adelaide from April 4-6 against the winner of the tie between India and the Czech Republic.
"That was one step, there are three more to go," Australia captain John Newcombe warned.
Sunday's dead reverse singles will see Woodforde play Pioline and Rafter meet Boetsch.
